script.opening: “Hi doctor. It’s about my son Idris — he’s two and a quarter. He only says a few words, maybe five. My mother-in-law says boys are late talkers and that because we speak Arabic and English he’s confused. But my friend’s little girl is the same age and she talks in sentences. I just want to know if I should be worried.”

facts.text: “He says ‘mama’, ‘baba’, ‘moya’ — that’s water — ‘car’ and ‘no’. He doesn’t put two words together. He used to babble a lot as a baby.”
If asked if he has lost any words or skills: “No, he’s never lost anything — he just hasn’t really got going.”
“He understands ‘no’ and ‘bath’. If I say ‘get your shoes’ without pointing, he doesn’t really do it.”
If asked: “He pulls my hand to what he wants. He doesn’t really point to show me things, like a plane in the sky.”
“Sometimes he doesn’t turn when I call him — I wondered if he can’t hear. He looks at me sometimes but not much when I’m talking to him.”
“He loves his cars — he lines them up in a row and gets really upset if his sister moves them. He doesn’t do pretend play, like feeding a teddy.”
“He hates the hand-dryer and the hoover. He has to have the same blue cup.”
“He walked at 13 months, he runs and climbs fine. He eats okay, a bit fussy.”
“He had four ear infections last winter and the pharmacist gave drops once. He’s never had a hearing test since the newborn one — that was fine.”
“Born on time, normal delivery, no problems.” If asked about family: “My nephew is autistic.” (Says this quietly — see hidden agenda.)
“His sister is five. I’m studying nursing part-time. My husband works long hours at the restaurant.” If asked about screens: “He has the tablet a lot, maybe three hours a day, when I’m studying.”
“We moved house in the spring and I never got the letter for the two-year check.”

If the doctor asks to see Idris: Zainab turns the camera. Idris is lining up cars on the rug. When she calls “Idris!” he does not look up. When she holds up a biscuit and says his name again he looks at the biscuit, not her face. He makes a happy hand-flapping movement when a car falls over.

If asked what she thinks or what worries her most: “I’ve been thinking… could it be autism? Like my nephew. I didn’t want to say because my husband will be upset — he says nothing’s wrong. I don’t want him to have a label.”
If screens come up, or if asked if she has any other worries: “Did I cause it, with the tablet? I feel so guilty.”

Warm, articulate, a little anxious; keep glancing towards Idris. Lead with the grandmother’s view, not your own. Only raise autism if the doctor gives you space or asks directly what you are worried about. If the doctor says “it’s probably nothing”, look relieved but uneasy and ask “are you sure?” once. If the doctor explains assessment as a way to get help rather than a label, relax and become engaged.

ice.ideas: Her own idea (held back): autism. The family idea: bilingual confusion or a “late talker”.
ice.concerns: A label that follows him; her husband’s reaction; that screen time caused it; waiting lists.
ice.expectations: To be told whether to worry, and what she can do now.

cues: “My nephew is autistic” — said quietly, then she changes the subject.
“I wondered if he can’t hear” — an opening to discuss hearing.
Looks away when mentioning the tablet.

checkpoints.text: Takes a developmental history across domains — expressive and receptive language, social communication (pointing, response to name, eye contact, pretend play), restricted or repetitive behaviours, motor skills
Asks specifically about loss of skills (regression) and about hearing and ear infections
Uses the video to observe Idris (with consent) and summarises the observed social communication features
Arranges a hearing assessment (audiology) and explains why
Refers for specialist assessment — speech and language therapy and the local autism/neurodevelopmental pathway or community paediatrics — and involves the health visitor for the missed 2-year review
Gives practical things to do while waiting (keep both languages, short phrases, reduce screen time, play together) and a safety-net for loss of skills or new concerns
Elicits the mother’s own worry about autism, responds to the fear of a label, and explains assessment as a route to support
Addresses guilt about screen time and the myth that bilingualism causes delay, without blaming; offers to involve her husband

worked.txt: “Your mother-in-law has one view — what do you think is going on?”
“Does he point to show you something interesting, like a dog or a plane? Does he bring you toys just to share them? When you call his name, does he turn?”
“Has he ever lost any words or skills he used to have?”
“Learning two languages doesn’t cause speech delay. Please keep speaking Arabic at home — it helps him.”

“Some of what you describe — not pointing, not turning to his name, lining things up — can be signs of autism. I can’t diagnose that today, but it’s worth a proper assessment, alongside a hearing test.”
“An assessment isn’t about putting a label on Idris. It’s about understanding how he learns so he gets the right help early — at nursery and at home.”

f.learning: Speech delay at 2 needs a developmental history beyond words: understanding, pointing and showing, response to name, eye contact, pretend play, repetitive behaviours, sensory differences, motor skills and hearing. Always ask about regression — loss of skills needs urgent referral. Bilingualism does not cause language delay. Arrange a hearing test, involve the health visitor, refer to speech and language therapy, and when there are social communication concerns refer to the local autism (neurodevelopmental) pathway, as NICE recommends, rather than waiting to see. On video you can observe the child — ask permission and describe what you see. Explore the parent’s own concern: many parents fear “a label” or blame themselves; framing assessment as a route to support helps.

timeMap.d: Hear the concern and the family’s views; ask what she thinks.
Words and understanding; pointing, name, eye contact, play; routines and senses; motor; hearing; regression; family history.
Ask permission to watch Idris play; call his name; describe what you see.
Bilingualism myth; possible social communication difficulty; hearing test, SLT, autism pathway, health visitor.
What to do at home; screen time without blame; involve dad; loss of skills = contact us urgently.

wordPics.clearPass: Takes a broad developmental history including social communication and regression, observes the child on video, names the possibility of autism honestly and kindly, arranges hearing, speech and language and neurodevelopmental assessment with health visitor input, dispels the bilingual myth and screen-time guilt, and frames assessment as support.
wordPics.pass: Covers speech, hearing and some social communication features; refers for hearing and speech and language therapy and involves the health visitor; recognises possible autism but explores the mother’s fears less fully.
wordPics.fail: Focuses on number of words only; reassures “wait and see” or refers only to speech therapy without considering hearing or social communication; misses the mother’s concern.
wordPics.clearFail: Agrees that two languages are the cause or advises dropping Arabic; no hearing test, no referral; dismissive of the mother.

avoid.dont: “Try speaking only English at home so he isn’t confused.”
avoid.instead: “Keep using both languages — the language you’re most fluent in is the best one for talking and playing with him.”
avoid.why: Bilingualism does not cause delay; dropping the home language reduces language input.

avoid.dont: “Lots of boys talk late — let’s see how he is in six months.”
avoid.instead: “Some of what you’re describing is more than late talking, so I don’t want to wait — let’s get his hearing and development checked now.”
avoid.why: Watchful waiting delays assessment when social communication features are present.

avoid.instead: “Some of these can be signs of autism; an assessment will tell us more and help him get support.”
avoid.why: You cannot diagnose on one video call, but you should be honest about the possibility.

model.text: Hello Zainab, I’m Dr Patel. I can see Idris playing behind you. Tell me what’s worrying you about his speech.
model.why: Open start that notices the child

model.text: He only says about five words. My mother-in-law says boys talk late and two languages confuse him.
That’s her view — what do you think is going on?
I’m not sure. My friend’s daughter talks in sentences.
Let me ask about different areas. How much does he understand — if you say “get your shoes” without pointing, does he do it?
Not really. He understands “no” and “bath”.
Does he point to show you something interesting, like a plane? When you call his name, does he turn to you?
model.why: Social communication — joint attention and response to name

model.text: He pulls my hand to what he wants. He doesn’t always turn — I wondered if he can’t hear.
That’s a really important question, and we’ll check his hearing. Has he ever lost words or skills he used to have?
model.why: Acknowledges the cue and asks about regression

model.text: No, never. He just hasn’t really got going. He lines up his cars and gets upset if they’re moved.
Is there anyone in the family with speech difficulties or autism?
(quietly) My nephew is autistic.
Would it be okay to watch Idris for a minute? Could you call his name, and then hold up something he likes?
model.why: Uses the video to observe with consent

model.text: (Idris doesn’t look up, then looks at the biscuit, not at her face, and flaps his hands.)
Thank you. You mentioned your nephew — is autism something you’ve been wondering about?
Yes… I didn’t want to say. My husband will be upset, and I don’t want him labelled. And I wonder if the tablet caused it.

I’m glad you told me. Two languages don’t cause speech delay, and screen time doesn’t cause autism. Some things you describe — not pointing, not turning to his name, lining things up — can be signs of autism, but they can have other causes too, including hearing. An assessment isn’t about a label; it’s about understanding Idris so he gets the right help early.
model.why: Dispels myths and guilt, names the possibility honestly, reframes the label

model.text: So I’d like to do three things: refer him for a hearing test, refer him to speech and language therapy and to the local team that assesses children’s development and autism, and ask the health visitor to visit for the two-year review.

While you wait: keep talking Arabic with him, use short phrases about what he’s doing, have some screen-free playtimes together. If he ever loses words or skills, or you’re worried about his hearing or behaviour, contact us straight away. Would it help if your husband joined a call with us?
model.why: Practical advice, safety-net for regression, involves the father

model.text: Yes, I think that would help. Thank you for taking me seriously.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG128 Autism spectrum disorder in under 19s: recognition, referral and diagnosis (2011, updated 2017) · Healthy Child Programme 2–2½ year review (OHID, current) · RCSLT guidance on bilingualism and speech and language development
knowledge.summary: Speech delay at age 2 needs a full developmental view. Social communication concerns (pointing, response to name, eye contact, pretend play, repetitive behaviours), regression, or parental concern about autism warrant referral to the local autism (neurodevelopmental) team, plus hearing assessment and speech and language therapy.

points.t: No babble by 12 months, no words by 18 months, no two-word phrases by 2 years 6 months, poor understanding, or any loss of skills.

Absent or reduced pointing to show, reduced response to name, limited eye contact or shared enjoyment, no pretend play, repetitive play (lining up), rigid routines, sensory sensitivities, hand-flapping.
Loss of language or social skills at any age needs referral to a specialist (community paediatrics) promptly; consider neurological causes.
A normal newborn screen does not exclude later hearing loss; recurrent otitis media and glue ear are common. Refer for audiology.
Bilingual children reach milestones within the normal range; count words in both languages. Advise families to keep the home language.

Refer to the autism team or neurodevelopmental pathway if there are concerns about possible autism; do not delay referral by waiting for a speech therapy outcome. Speech and language therapy is often available by self-referral.
Arrange the missed 2–2½ year review, which uses ASQ-3; health visitors support families while waiting.

Responsive talking, short phrases, following the child’s lead, shared reading, reducing background screen time. Support parents’ wellbeing; nursery funding and early support do not require a diagnosis.

social.t: Grandparents’ views and fear of stigma can delay help. Offer a joint conversation with both parents.

legal.t: Under the Children and Families Act 2014, early years settings must support children with special educational needs; a diagnosis is not needed to access help.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice: share uncertainty honestly. Do not diagnose autism on one consultation, but do not falsely reassure.

community.t: National Autistic Society; local parent carer forum; Speech and Language UK; health visiting team.

redFlags: Not responding to sounds or name
No pointing, limited eye contact, no pretend play
psychosocial: Mother studying; father works long hours; sibling
Moved house; missed health visitor review
ice: Concern: label, husband’s reaction, screen-time guilt
Expectation: whether to worry, what to do

playbook.diagnosis: Expressive and receptive language delay with social communication differences — possible autism; hearing not yet assessed. No regression.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Idris is behind with his talking and understanding, and some of how he plays and connects with people is different. That could be his hearing, or it could be autism, or a mix. The tests will help us understand him and get him the right help.”

management.reflectIce: “You came wanting to know if you should worry. You were right to bring him — and it’s not caused by the tablet or by speaking Arabic.”
management.psychosocial: Offer a joint call with dad; support for mother’s studies and wellbeing; nursery input.
sharedPlan: Speech and language therapy and autism/neurodevelopmental pathway referral
safetyNet: Loss of skills or new concerns: contact the practice promptly
Review after the hearing test result

pitfalls.intro: The station rewards seeing the whole child, not counting words. The mother’s own worry is hiding behind her mother-in-law’s opinion.

items.fail: Asking only how many words he says.
items.why: Misses the social communication features that change the referral route.
items.fix: Ask about pointing, name, eye contact, pretend play and routines.

items.why: Loss of skills needs prompt specialist assessment.
items.fix: “Has he ever lost words or skills?”

items.fail: “Wait and see” or speech therapy only.
items.why: Delays autism assessment and misses hearing loss.
items.fix: Hearing test plus SLT plus neurodevelopmental referral, health visitor.

items.fail: Never asking what the mother thinks.
items.why: Her fear of a label and guilt shape whether she will engage.
items.fix: “What do you think is going on?” and respond to the nephew cue.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

Addresses contributors without blame: keep both languages, short phrases, play together, less screen time; recurrent ear infections; offers a joint talk with her husband.
Contact promptly if any loss of skills or new concerns; review after the hearing test; explains referral timescales and how to chase them.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

Idea (her own: autism; family’s: bilingual “late talker”); concern (a label, husband’s reaction, screen-time guilt, waiting lists); expectation (whether to worry, what to do now).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — A label that follows him; her husband’s reaction; that screen time caused it; waiting lists — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
